That ability should be exercised and expanded with education, but it isn't necessarily, and in fact, in many cases (and particularly in the US), it is, if anything, discouraged by education. To the detriment of the people (and the not coincidental advantage of the empowered few), there's virtually no emphasis in US education on considering and understanding ideas and being able to reason effectively. Instead, virtually all of the emphasis is on simply memorizing and regurgitating on command a particular narrow set of pre-approved positions and dissociated factoids, and if anything, that actually encourages intolerance.

If we're considering "education" in an ideal sense, then yes - that's probably accurate. Intolerance is primarily a defense mechanism that allows people who don't want to have to consider ideas that might undermine their presumptions to reject them out of hand, and a truly well-educated person - which is to say, a person who's been given a lot of data to work with and has been taught to seek out whatever information might apply and to reason effectively - generally has neither need nor desire to do that. My freshman year of college you had two required classes.

First semester was a psychology class, but it wasn't your typical Psych 101, regurgitate these facts. It was all about how people think, how they learn, how memory works, how different people learn different ways, and how our experiences sometimes affects our future decisions. No text book, just meeting people who could memorize a lot of shit, seeing magic tricks and learning how you things like misdirection works, the teacher giving a normal lecture only to have someone grab a bag and run out of the room -- now describe the thief? it was all set up, to show you how faulty your memory can be. Stuff like that.

It was fucking fascinating.

Second semester was a Sociology class. Again, it wasn't simple regurgitation. The first day they said, last semester we taught you about thinking. This semester is about how we interact as a society.

One of my biggest memories is about Tower Building Day. The first rule of TBD is you do not talk about TBD out of class, because it ruins it for future class takers. (This was years before Fight Club. Maybe the guy who wrote Fight Club had a Tower Building Day. I dunno.)

The week before TBD they told you, "Next week is Tower Building Day, bring supplies." And that's all they'd say. They wouldn't answer when you asked WTF that meant.

On TBD people brought all kinds of shit. Boxes, legos, wood, parts of furniture. There were 30 of us in the class, so they separated us into 6 teams. One team was taken away and put into a seperate room. Then the other 5 were told "build a tower in 15 minutes."

Then the 6th team came back to judge the towers and declare a winner. They gave us surveys: How do you feel about winning or losing? How do you feel about the team that won?

Then they told us, the winner was picked before the judges even saw your towers. Then they asked "how do you feel about shit now?"

IT was fucking fascinating. Long story short (TOO LATE) it was about how our experiences and expectations can change how we see those around us and how we interact and feel about them.

This stuff sticks with you much better and longer than just barfing facts back up.
